title: Recognising Producer Styles
quiz.0.question: In which decade did the Barolo Boys revolution begin?
quiz.0.explanation: The Barolo Boys revolution began in the 1980s, when modernist winemakers such as Elio Altare introduced French barriques and new techniques, challenging the traditionalists.
quiz.1.question: What casks do traditional Barolo producers mainly use?
quiz.1.explanation: Traditionalists use large Slavonian oak casks (botti) of 20-100 hL, which add almost no oak aroma and preserve a pure expression of terroir.
quiz.2.question: Which MGA do the grapes for Giacomo Conterno's Monfortino come from?
quiz.2.explanation: The grapes for Monfortino come from Giacomo Conterno's Cascina Francia vineyard in Serralunga d'Alba (the Francia MGA) — a legend among legends; Vigna Rionda is a separate MGA in Serralunga.
quiz.3.question: In blind tasting, how can you quickly tell traditional from modern Barolo?
quiz.3.options.0: Look at the appellation on the label
quiz.3.options.1: Observe the depth of colour and the oak influence
quiz.3.explanation: Depth of colour (paler in traditional wines) and oak influence (obvious vanilla and chocolate in modern wines) are the most direct clues.
slides.0.title: Recognising Producer Styles
slides.0.subtitle: Traditional vs modern — the Barolo style wars and the great estates in depth
slides.1.title: The Barolo Style Wars (1980-2010)
slides.1.content:
In the 1980s Elio Altare brought French barrique techniques back from Burgundy, sparking the fiercest style debate in the history of Italian wine.

Traditionalists (Tradizionalisti)

  • Casks: large Slavonian oak casks (botti, 20-100 hL), with almost no oak aroma
  • Maceration: 30-60 days (very long extraction)
  • Colour: pale garnet with a brick rim (even when young)
  • Aromas: dried rose, tar, leather, tobacco
  • Tannins: rough and grippy, needing 15-20 years to be ready
  • Leading names: Giacomo Conterno, Bartolo Mascarello, Bruno Giacosa

Modernists (the Barolo Boys)

  • Casks: small French oak barrels (barrique, 225 L), adding vanilla and chocolate
  • Maceration: 10-20 days (shorter, keeping fruit)
  • Colour: deep garnet, almost opaque
  • Aromas: fresh berries, vanilla, chocolate, coffee
  • Tannins: smooth and fine, enjoyable after 5-10 years
  • Leading names: Elio Altare, Luciano Sandrone, Roberto Voerzio, Gaja
slides.2.title: Top Producers in Depth
slides.2.content:
Giacomo Conterno — King of the Traditionalists

Philosophy: "Barolo is born to age, not to be drunk young" | committed to very large botti (50-100 hL)
Flagship: Monfortino (the Francia vineyard in Serralunga) | made only in outstanding vintages | about 7 years in large casks before release | ages 30-50 years
Entry point: Barolo Francia (formerly Cascina Francia) | an earlier-released wine from the same site | ready after 10 years | better value

Luciano Sandrone — Legend of the Modernists

Legend: once a cellar worker at Marchesi di Barolo, he bought his first plot of Cannubi Boschis in 1977 and built a world-class estate from nothing
Flagship: Barolo Cannubi Boschis (renamed Aleste from the 2013 vintage) | aged in 500-litre French tonneaux | powerful yet silky tannins
Recent shift: gentler extraction and more restrained oak, showing a move from modernist to fusion style
slides.3.title: Blind-Tasting Recognition Skills
slides.3.content:
Using three levels — sight, smell and palate — you can systematically tell traditional from modern Barolo:

1. Look at the colour: traditional wines show a brick rim even when young (pale garnet); young modern wines have a purple rim (deep garnet)
2. Smell for oak: obvious vanilla, chocolate, toast → modern (small French barrels); almost no oak, only tar, rose and leather → traditional (large casks)
3. Test the tannins: if a young wine (under 5 years) already has smooth tannins → modern; rough, grippy tannins → traditional. Traditional wines need 15-20 years to peak, modern ones 8-12
4. The fusion phenomenon: since 2000 the mainstream has moved to the neo-traditionalists — modern facilities (temperature control, hygiene) but traditional large casks and longer maceration. Vietti, G.D. Vajra and Massolino are examples
slides.4.title: Style Divides in Other Areas
slides.4.content:
Brunello di Montalcino

Traditional vs modern

Traditional: Biondi-Santi, Soldera, long ageing in large Slavonian casks, elegant and high in acid, needing long ageing / Modern: Casanova di Neri, Siro Pacenti, small French barrels, rich fruit, earlier drinking

Chianti Classico

Traditional vs modern

Traditional: Montevertine, Badia a Coltibuono, Sangiovese with native grapes such as Canaiolo and Colorino, aged in large casks, light and high in acid / Modern: some estates age in small French barrels and blend in Cabernet or Merlot, rich and international

Franciacorta DOCG

Sparkling style divide

Elegant school: Bellavista, Ca' del Bosco, long lees contact (36-60 months), delicate mineral complexity / Fruit-driven school: shorter lees contact (at least 18 months by law for non-vintage), fresh and approachable
slides.5.title: 🍷 Style Example: Traditional Barolo
slides.5.caption: G.D. Vajra Barolo 2006 — an estate known for ageing in traditional large Slavonian casks, following a style close to Giacomo Conterno and Bartolo Mascarello.
slides.6.title: 🍷 Style Example: Modern Barolo
slides.6.caption: Parusso Mariondino Barolo 2010 — a modernist estate known for ageing in small French barrels (barriques), with rich fruit and softer tannins.
slides.7.title: Key Takeaways
slides.7.points.0: The Barolo style wars (1980-2010): Elio Altare brought French barriques back from Burgundy, sparking the traditionalist vs modernist debate
slides.7.points.1: Traditional traits: large Slavonian casks (botti), 30-60 days' maceration, pale brick colour, rough tannins, needing 15-20 years' ageing
slides.7.points.2: Modern traits: small French barrels (barriques), 10-20 days' maceration, deep purple colour, smooth tannins, ready after 5-10 years
slides.7.points.3: Giacomo Conterno's Monfortino is the king of the traditionalists (made only in outstanding vintages, ages 30-50 years)
slides.7.points.4: Luciano Sandrone is the modernist legend (a cellar worker who built his estate from nothing, ageing Cannubi Boschis — now Aleste — in 500-litre tonneaux)
slides.7.points.5: Blind-tasting keys: colour of the rim (brick vs purple) + oak influence (none vs obvious vanilla and chocolate) + tannin texture
slides.7.points.6: Since 2000 the mainstream has been the fusion school (neo-traditionalists): modern technology + traditional philosophy, with Vietti and Massolino as examples
slides.7.points.7: Brunello, Chianti and Franciacorta have similar traditional vs modern style divides
slides.7.points.8: Which style to choose is a personal preference: traditional suits cellaring, modern suits earlier enjoyment
